title: Unit testing
body:
Testing one unit (a single method or class) in isolation, automatically, with everything it
depends on either stubbed out or trivially available. It is the bottom of the testing
hierarchy and the one that pays for itself, because it runs in seconds and points at the
exact line that broke.

This is what the [[Object Oriented Approach]] means by **reliability** in its benefits list,
and it is only cheap if [[Coupling and Cohesion]] is good: a class that can only be
constructed by starting the whole system is a class you cannot unit test, so untestable code
is a design report, not a testing problem.

## Shape of a test

Arrange, act, assert. Set up the input, call the one thing under test, check the result
against an expected value.

```java
@Test
public void popReturnsMostRecentlyPushed() {
    Stack<Integer> s = new Stack<>();   // arrange
    s.push(1);
    s.push(2);
    assertEquals(2, s.pop());           // act + assert
}
```

One behaviour per test. A test that asserts six things tells you six things might be wrong
and does not say which.

## What to actually test

Not "every method". Test the behaviour at the boundaries, which is where the defects are:
empty input, one element, full, the maximum, one past the maximum, null, negative. The middle
of the range almost never fails on its own. [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] is where this pays
off most visibly: off-by-one on an [[Array]] boundary is the standard bug and the standard
test.

## Levels above it

- **Integration testing**: the units together, checking the interfaces between them. No note
  in the vault; not covered as its own topic.
- **System testing**: the whole thing against the [[Specification]].
- **Acceptance testing**: the customer confirming it is what they asked for, which closes the
  loop back to [[Software Requirements Analysis]].

## Why it matters more than it looks

A defect costs more the later it is found ([[SDLC]]). Unit tests are the earliest automated
point that exists. They are also what makes change safe: without them, every response to a
[[Code Smells|code smell]] is a gamble, so the design quietly stops improving and
[[Complexity]] only ever goes up. Automated tests are a precondition for [[Agile]] for exactly
this reason, since the code is re-tested every iteration.

What unit tests cannot do is tell you the requirement was wrong. They encode the author's
intent, so a misunderstanding passes cleanly. That is [[Review]]'s job.

Related: [[Exception Handling]], [[Metrics]].
